title: Phone vs laptop: which save wins?

titles: Phone vs Laptop: Which Save Wins? (Out-of-Order Writes)
Why Your App Sent You Back an Hour
publish.description: Two devices save your progress, and one morning you're an hour behind. Why the last save to arrive isn't the newest, and the conditional update that keeps the right one.
extra: 🎬 The full video (from one laptop to a million students: local storage, progress on the server, 20k writes per second and two devices that disagree) is on the channel.
A conditional update (write only if newer) is a condition expression in DynamoDB, a WHERE clause in SQL, a Lua script in Redis; in Cassandra, write with USING TIMESTAMP set to when the save happened.

scenes.heading: Phone vs laptop: *which save wins?*
scenes.narration: You study on the laptop at night, and on the phone on the bus. Both save your progress. One morning you open the app, and you're an hour behind. Which save won, and why?

scenes.title: Out of order
scenes.narration: On the bus, the phone has no signal, so its saves wait. At home, the laptop moves you on to lesson four. Then the phone reconnects and sends lesson three, from an hour ago. The last save to arrive wins, so lesson three wins. You go back an hour.

note.text: Last to arrive wins → *you go back*

scenes.title: Keep the newest
scenes.narration: The fix: every save carries when it happened. The store keeps it only if it's newer than what it has, in one atomic step: check and write together. The late save from the phone is ignored.

scenes.title: What it costs
scenes.narration: The cost: device clocks can be wrong. So the phone sends how long ago each save happened, and the server subtracts that from its own clock. Some apps also just ask: lesson four, or lesson three?

scenes.title: When, not arrival
scenes.narration: Order saves by when they happened, not by when they arrived. Would you pick automatically, or ask the user? The full video is on the channel.

notes: "Last write wins" in databases like Cassandra or DynamoDB usually means the highest timestamp wins, which is exactly the fix here when the timestamp is when the save happened. The bug is ordering by arrival.

A conditional update keeps the newest in one atomic step: UPDATE ... WHERE saved_at < :new in SQL, a condition expression in DynamoDB, a Lua script in Redis. In Cassandra a conditional write is a lightweight transaction (Paxos, several round trips), so the cheap way is writing with USING TIMESTAMP = saved_at.

Device clocks drift or are set wrong, so never compare two devices' clock times. Use the device clock only to measure durations: the phone sends how long ago each save happened, and the server turns that into its own time. The limit: that elapsed time resets if the phone restarts while offline. Alternative: version numbers; each save carries the version it read, and the server rejects an old version, which becomes a conflict or a question to the user.
Some apps resolve it by asking; e-readers, for example, offer to jump to the furthest page read on another device.
The same rule applies when the app opens: local copy versus server copy, the newest by when it happened wins.
Overwriting the whole row would also discard quiz answers the phone saved for another lesson. Storing and comparing per lesson avoids it.
